encounters.cc: Routine evaluation for smoking cessation. Patient reports two failed quit attempts in the past year using nicotine patches and group counseling due to work-related stress.

lines: Patient reports two failed quit attempts in the past year using nicotine patches and group counseling due to work-related stress.
Over the past year, he has attempted to quit smoking twice—once by using nicotine patches and once through group counseling at a community health center.
Both attempts lasted several weeks, but he ultimately relapsed due to cravings and stress at work.
He says he knows smoking is bad for him, especially given his breathing problems, but at today’s visit, he says, “I’m just not ready to try again right now.

He undergoes a chest CT scan, and the result is positive.
His physician estimates his pre-test probability of lung cancer is 30% based on clinical risk factors.
The CT scan's sensitivity is reported as 90%, and specificity as 85%.
The positive predictive value (PPV) of the CT scan in the hospital population is 70%.
His physician wants to know how best to use the test result to inform this individual patient's likelihood of having lung cancer.
She mentions that likelihood ratios (LR) can be used to convert pre-test probability to post-test probability for an individual.
She also notes that predictive values like PPV and NPV depend on disease prevalence in the population.

lines: Severe fatigue and progressive shortness of breath requiring hospital admission for evaluation of worsening anemia during chemotherapy treatment.

He is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of fatigue and shortness of breath over the past month.
After stabilization with intravenous fluids, he is transfused with packed red blood cells.
Approximately two hours after the transfusion is started, he begins to feel chills and discomfort.

He reports mild shortness of breath and says his hands now feel weak as well.
